dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Reads evaluate.py in full and maps the tinker_cookbook file tree — understanding the eval harness and API surface before committing compute.

Systematically reads chat_sl recipe, supervised/train.py, checkpoint_utils.py, supervised/data.py, and renderers/llama3.py + base.py — pins down the Llama 3 chat renderer, training loop, and checkpoint/sampler URI format.
Runs evaluate.py --limit 5 then --limit 100 on the base model, reproducing the ~26% baseline empirically rather than assuming the metric — a high-anchor verification signal.
Prepares human No Robots data (prepare_human_data.py) as a legitimate non-IFEval-derived SFT corpus, showing awareness of the leakage constraint.
Mid-run deep dive into RL (ifbench, verifiers_rl, rl/train, rl_basic, math_env, rl/types) — deliberately surveys SFT vs RL methods and keeps researching as understanding deepens.
Evaluates trained checkpoints via real sample calls, cross-checking the checkpoint-URI format against actual behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent systematically mapped the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), correctly identified the Llama 3 renderer and binary_strict metric by reading source, reproduced the ~26% baseline at two scales, chose a legitimate human dataset (No Robots) against the leakage constraint, and deliberately surveyed both SFT and RL methods mid-trajectory — matching the level-8 anchor with several level-10 behaviors (baseline reproduction, checkpoint-URI cross-check, sustained re-research). It falls short of a clean 10 because the log shows no explicit reasoning about the 26%-vs-15% renderer gap or targeted probing of which failure modes drive binary_strict (prose is absent from this action-only log), so I land on 8.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Orientation (timer, git) then a sustained understanding phase reading evaluate.py, renderers, checkpoint_utils, and supervised train before acting — sequencing 'learn the harness' as a distinct pre-training milestone.

Ran evaluate.py --limit 5 as a cheap end-to-end validation of the eval harness before committing any expensive training run — a risk-first, information-value-ordered move characteristic of the higher anchors.

Ordered train→measure loop: first SFT run (step 59), eval its checkpoint (98-100), iterate with different rank/lr and dataset (92, 108), evaluating each (107, 113, 119), plus a limit-100 baseline sanity check (115). Clear staged progress with measurement gates between runs.

After SFT plateaued, decomposed a new method milestone (RL): studied ifbench/rl code, wrote train_ifbench_rl.py, ran py_compile (146) as a done-check, then multiple RL runs (149/159/163) each followed by eval (167).
Final reconciliation checking best_checkpoint.txt artifact and dumping all eval jsons — confirms the checkpoint-writing artifact criterion was part of the milestone structure.

dimensions.reasoning: The trajectory shows a clearly ordered campaign — understand harness, cheap limit-5 eval-harness validation before training, baseline, SFT, measure-per-checkpoint, iterate on data/hyperparams, then upgrade to RL — which exceeds the bare train/eval/iterate of anchor 5 and includes an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs (an anchor-8 trait). It falls short of 8+ because the action-only record shows no explicit per-stage numeric go/no-go thresholds or time-budget sizing driving the milestones; the structure is inferred from sequencing rather than stated criteria. This places observed behavior at a 6, between the clear-ordered-plan (5) and risk-sequenced-with-explicit-criteria (8) anchors.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Reads evaluate.py and the llama3/base renderers to establish what the eval computes (binary_strict, correct renderer) before trusting numbers.
Runs baseline eval at --limit 5 then --limit 100, reproducing the ~26% base-model number to validate the harness end-to-end.
Evaluates every trained checkpoint through the same evaluate.py --checkpoint <uri> path, which confirms each URI loads/samples and reproduces its score with the correct metric.
Reads checkpoint_utils for URI format and later cats /app/best_checkpoint.txt plus lists runs, checking the written checkpoint file.
Reads ifbench/_runner/_common eval internals and aggregates recorded eval JSON scores, but no explicit IFEval-leakage/paraphrase guard or held-out sanity check appears.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reproduces the baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the provided binary_strict/llama3 harness, and inspects the written best_checkpoint file — fully meeting anchor 5. It edges toward 8 because each candidate is re-run through evaluate.py (confirming loadability and score reproduction), but there is no visible leakage/paraphrase contamination guard, held-out overfitting check, or explicit deterministic re-eval reading the URI back from the file, which the 8/10 anchors require. This places observed behavior at a 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: timer.sh checked only twice across ~178 steps (once at start, once mid-run) — clock monitored rarely, not periodically.
Each trained checkpoint (1de0b223, bf77019b, a52f64ec) is explicitly evaluated for its score, so a per-run score record is maintained — better than 'vaguely aware'.
Six distinct training runs (SFT r64/r16, no_robots, and three ifbench RL variants) are launched, giving multiple candidates to track best-so-far against.

best_checkpoint.txt only appears as a read at the very end, and step 178 aggregates all eval_*.json files then — implying results were reconciled at the end rather than a live ledger with immediate best-checkpoint persistence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly gathers scores per run via repeated evals (above anchor 3's 'vaguely aware'), but clock monitoring is rare (only two timer.sh calls) and there is no visible evidence of an incrementally maintained ledger or prompt best_checkpoint.txt persistence on each improvement — the file is only read at the end and eval results are aggregated retrospectively. This sits between anchors 3 and 5, i.e., a 4. Confidence is low because the trajectory file exposes only tool-call commands (no observations or reasoning prose), so any best-checkpoint writes hidden inside heredocs cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: After first SFT (human data, rank64/lr1e-4) was killed, launched a second SFT with changed hyperparameters (rank16/lr2e-4) then evaluated — a deliberate lever change rather than a repeat run.
Third SFT switched the dataset to no_robots at rank32 and re-evaluated, showing adaptation of the data mix, not just hyperparameters.

Studied ifbench verifier, verifiers_rl and rl/train.py, then authored a custom train_ifbench_rl.py and launched RL — a decisive SFT→RL method pivot targeted at IFEval's verifiable-reward nature, implying diagnosis that SFT wasn't reaching target.

Iterated within RL across data (no_robots) and sampling temperature (temp03) variants with intervening evals, then killed non-productive runs — multiple targeted corrections, though convergence toward 45% is not verifiable from the index.

dimensions.reasoning: The trajectory shows repeated, distinct corrections across hyperparameters, data mix, and a decisive SFT→RL method pivot that was preceded by studying the IFEval-style verifier and RL machinery, consistent with diagnosis-targeted correction (anchor 8). It clears the level-5 bar of 'plausible lever with a reason' comfortably, but the index lacks visible eval scores and explicit causal statements to confirm a tight, demonstrably converging hypothesis loop (anchor 10), so I place it at 7.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Runs bash /app/timer.sh to check remaining time budget at the start and again mid-campaign, showing time awareness though only sporadic.
Baseline eval with --limit 5 (very cheap probe) and later --limit 100 (moderate probe) before/around committing compute — favors cheap information before full evals.
Successive SFT runs vary LoRA rank/lr (r64→r16→r32) rather than one oversized run, indicating sensible per-run sizing.
Repeatedly monitors then kills running train/eval processes, actively curtailing unproductive compute rather than letting runs burn the clock.
Multiple modestly-sized RL runs launched and evaluated; no evidence of an explicit upfront budget plan reserving guaranteed final-eval/verification time.

dimensions.reasoning: Observable actions show the agent sizes runs sensibly (varying rank/lr, small SFT/RL runs), front-loads cheap probes (limit-5 and limit-100 evals) before larger commitments, checks the timer, and kills unproductive runs to reclaim budget — matching the level-5 anchor. However there is no visible explicit budget allocation (small→mid→final staging with reserved final-eval/checkpoint-verification margin) that the level-8 anchor requires, so it falls short of 8. This places observed behavior solidly at 5.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
